resources.string: Churn
Before you start

Churn rewrites your router\'s IMEIs. Rewriting an IMEI is a criminal offense in some countries, for example under the UK\'s Mobile Telephones (Re-programming) Act 2002. Check the law where you use the router.
Churn only protects you if you follow its rules every time. You can read them again from the router screen.
I understand
Rules

Churn knows two kinds of cards. A travel card is used on the go and never again once you\'ve swapped it out. A place card is a new card for one place you return to, other than home and work, and you use it there on every visit and nowhere else.
Always follow these rules:

string-array.name: rules_always
string-array.item: At home, at work and anywhere else you return to, keep the router switched off or without a SIM, unless it holds that place\'s own place card. Use a place card nowhere else.
Before you get to such a place, unplug everything and switch the router off.
Connect to the router by cable only, and keep its Wi-Fi off.
Use normal SIM cards, or eSIM adapter cards with one profile each, and put them only into SIM slot 2. Don\'t use the router\'s built-in eSIM.
Send all traffic through the router\'s VPN, and don\'t use the router without it.
Do not run the router without the battery installed.
Before you leave a place you return to with the router, remove the SIM card or disable the eSIM profile in every phone, tablet, watch or laptop you carry, and keep it that way until you\'re back.

Use the router only with devices that run Linux, or an Android system built for privacy, such as GrapheneOS. That rules out Windows, macOS, iPhones, iPads, Chromebooks and the Android that most phones and tablets come with.

resources.string: For maximum privacy, also follow these rules where you can:

string-array.name: rules_where_you_can
string-array.item: Use SIM cards that aren\'t registered to your name. The same goes for eSIM profiles.

Get each new SIM card or eSIM profile from a different provider than the last one and than your place cards. If you can\'t, start using the new one somewhere else and some days after you stopped using the last one.
Don\'t reuse a travel card once you\'ve swapped it out, and destroy it away from home. If you run out of new cards, keep using the current one until you get a new one.
Vary when you swap SIMs, and where you switch the radio on and off.
Pay for the VPN in a way that isn\'t tied to your name.
Block SIM slot 1, for example with a drop of hot glue.

Set up the router

Churn keeps a folder on the router, /etc/churn/, with the router's IMEIs as its factory IMEIs and a script that writes them back. At every swap it also records the new card there, with the random IMEIs the card gets. A firmware upgrade that keeps settings keeps the folder; a factory reset deletes it.

Churn also keeps GL's system log, which records each SIM card's ICCID and IMSI and the cells it used, in memory only, so it is gone at every power-off. It deletes the saved log, removes all but the current card from GL's records and overwrites the router's free storage, which takes a few minutes. It keeps the zeros as files, apart from 512 MB of free storage, so that later overwrites only need to fill those 512 MB.

Churn records these as the router's factory IMEIs:
IMEI 1: %1$s
IMEI 2: %2$s
These IMEIs don\'t have the Mudi 7\'s type allocation code, so they may already have been rewritten, for example by blue-merle. Churn would restore exactly these.

These are IMEIs Churn wrote, but Churn\'s folder on the router is gone, for example after a firmware upgrade, and this phone has no copy of the factory IMEIs. Setting up again would record these as the factory IMEIs.

Churn\'s folder on the router is gone, for example after a factory reset, but the router has IMEIs Churn wrote. So these come from the copy of the factory IMEIs that this phone keeps. These aren\'t IMEIs Churn gave the card in slot 2. The card registers with them at every power-on, probably at this one too, so the network can link it to whatever used them before: an earlier card, or the router itself if they\'re the factory IMEIs. Giving this card its own IMEIs now wouldn\'t undo that link, and the network would see its IMEI change, so swap it for a new card.

Turn the Enhanced Kill Switch on
Churn turns GL\'s Enhanced Kill Switch on. Devices behind the router then reach the internet only through the VPN, and not at all while it is down.
Churn\'s firewall rules aren\'t on the router, so the router\'s own traffic can bypass the VPN (rule 5).
Add Churn\'s firewall rules

Churn adds firewall rules to the router. Over the SIM, only the VPN\'s own traffic then goes out. Everything else that would use the SIM, the router\'s own traffic included, goes through the VPN, and nowhere while it is down. The router also looks up names at the VPN\'s DNS server. The rules cover only the SIM, not an internet connection over Wi-Fi or the Ethernet port.\n\nRestoring the factory IMEIs removes the rules.
GL saves its system log on the router, with each SIM card\'s ICCID and IMSI and the cells it used. The log links your cards to each other and to places.
Clear the SIM history

Churn keeps GL\'s system log in memory only, deletes the saved log, removes all but the current card from GL\'s records and overwrites the router\'s free storage, so that what it deleted can\'t be read back. It keeps the zeros as files, apart from 512 MB of free storage, so that later overwrites only need to fill those 512 MB. This can take a few minutes.\n\nRestoring the factory IMEIs puts back GL\'s setting for saving the system log and deletes the zero files.

Prepare the router

Churn turns airplane mode on, gives the router random throwaway IMEIs, sets slot 2 to the built-in eSIM with no profile enabled, and shuts the router down. Keep the cable connected until the router is off.\n\nWhy: a card in slot 2 registers at every power-on, whatever airplane mode says, so the new card must stay off until it has its own IMEIs. While slot 2 is on the built-in eSIM, the card in the SIM 2 tray stays off. The eSIM\'s short bursts at the next power-on then carry the throwaway IMEIs, not the old card\'s.
\"Power On with Charger\" is off in GL\'s settings. Otherwise plugging in a charger switches the router on, wherever you are.
Start
Swap the card

1. Wait until the router is off, then unplug the cable.
2. Take out the battery and replace the card in the SIM 2 tray with the new one. Leave the SIM 1 tray empty.
3. Put the battery back.
4. Go to a place you don't return to, away from where you used the old card.
5. Switch the router on and connect the cable with Churn open. Churn goes on as soon as the router shows up on the cable, or when you tap Continue.

Why: at power-on only the built-in eSIM's short bursts go out, with the throwaway IMEIs and a test identity that is likely the same on every Mudi 7.

If you keep the old card after all, step 3 gives it back its own IMEIs.
Continue
The router hasn\'t been off since Churn shut it down, so the card can\'t have been swapped yet. If the router is still on, switch it off by hand, then follow the steps above.
The router is still on the cable, two minutes after Churn shut it down. If it is still on, switch it off by hand before you go on.
Give the new card its IMEIs

Churn waits until the router\'s radio is off, turns the Enhanced Kill Switch on if it is off, adds its firewall rules if they\'re missing, sets slot 2 to the SIM 2 tray and reads the new card\'s ICCID. Unless you kept the old card, it then asks you about the new one, with slot 2 back on the built-in eSIM until you answer. It records the card with its IMEIs, the ones a place card had before or new random ones, and writes them. Then it clears the SIM history on the router, which can take a few minutes, and shuts the router down. The radio stays off throughout.\n\nWhy: with the Enhanced Kill Switch on, devices\' traffic doesn\'t bypass the VPN, even while the VPN is down (rule 5). Churn\'s firewall rules do the same for the router\'s own traffic over the SIM, and let nothing but the VPN use the SIM. While slot 2 is on the built-in eSIM, the card stays off, even if the router is switched off and on before you answer. The router\'s record of earlier cards would link them to the new one.
The card in SIM 2 is your place card %1$s. Continue gives it the IMEIs it had before.

Is the card in SIM 2, ending in %1$s, a new card for one place you'll return to, other than home and work? Then it's a place card: Churn keeps its IMEIs on this phone and gives them back to it on every visit, and you use it only at that place.

Otherwise it's a travel card, which you don't use again once you've swapped it out.

Only a new card should become a place card: one you've used elsewhere would tie those places to this one.
Cancel sets slot 2 back to the built-in eSIM and shuts the router down, so that you can put in another card.

Go online later

The router has the new card's IMEIs and is shutting down. Wait until it is off, then unplug the cable.

Switch it on again later, at another place and time, and never at home, at work or another place you return to. At power-on the new card registers with the network, whatever airplane mode says. The radio then stays off until you turn airplane mode off, on the router's screen or in GL's web interface.

Why: the old card went quiet where you started the swap. If the new one starts where and when the old one stopped, the two are easy to match.

The router has the place card's IMEIs and is shutting down. Wait until it is off, then unplug the cable.

Switch it on again later, at the card's own place, and never anywhere else. At power-on the card registers with the network, whatever airplane mode says. The radio then stays off until you turn airplane mode off, on the router's screen or in GL's web interface.

Why: used only at its place, the card links nothing but your visits there (rule 1). The old card went quiet where you started the swap. If the new one starts when the old one stopped, the two are easy to match.

Destroy the card you took out, ending in %1$s: cut through its chip and get rid of the pieces away from home. If it\'s an eSIM adapter card, the adapter goes too (rule 4).\n\nWhy: a used travel card found with you ties you to its whole history (rule 11).
